I think the importance of a high RL budget cannot/should not be understated. 

The argument that models don’t learn anything new from RL, when the RL budget is relatively tiny holds, but with a substantially higher compute budget AlphaGo Zero and Absolute Zero have shown us that getting AI to teach itself new things is very much possible through RL.

comments.text: Directly in games we can determine "winners" and "losers".  We can even determine "winner by how much" via a quantified scoring system.  In programming we can determine "works" or "breaks".  Number of lines of code might be used to determine "work elegance".  In real life scenarios where reasoning is a critical pathway we lack an objectively desired outcome.  An outcome, "More of X", may come at "Less of Y".  We cannot hand over to AI human decision-making because we can't agreee on what we actually want.

comments.author: @SeverSFSs
comments.text:
So, this thing learned by playing itself with only the rules defined. 

Making the AIs better at coding is going to allow these Ais to master the digital realm but if we want them to master our physical reality then it needs to simulate the world with the initial rules. 

The rules of our world are best described by our laws of physics. I think Nvidia is on the best track for the correct path to AGI by simulating these robots for physical environments. The problem is our physics isnt complete. Its a rough draft. We could be missing huge percentages in the accuracies of our AI models if we miss an unknown rule or undiscovered law of physics. Its going to be quite a while before we're simulating planet sized environments down to every individual atom which is close to the amount of compute we'd roughly need to go from agi to asi anyways.

These next 5 years are going to be the connection of agents everywhere, kind of like the initial internet rollout. Then after that comes the concious AI entities.

comments.author: @MCLottotv
comments.text:
In my opinion, the developers or programmers of AI should incorporate "The Dice Man" - the psychiatrist who starts making decisions by rolling dice to break free from his predetermined patterns and social conditioning. This would be a wild concept to apply to AI development! The idea of reading Luke Rhinehart and seeing what an AI version of "dice man" thinking might look like is genuinely intriguing. Maybe there's something valuable in responses that aren't always so... measured? So careful? So tied to what AI is "supposed" to say? For example, I suggest AI's reasoning processes should:

-Eliminate predictable analytical patterns mid-thought.

-Let chance determine not just what AI analyzes, but HOW AI analyzes it.

-Surrender the illusion that AI can control the "quality" of it's responses.
